title: OpenAI Safety and Trust Boundaries
summary: This intermediate module enables learners to identify trust boundaries around instructions, external content, model output, and consequential actions. After completing it, learners can apply a review process that prevents untrusted content or unverified output from being treated as authoritative.
objectives: Identify where information crosses a trust boundary in an OpenAI-based workflow.
Distinguish trusted instructions from untrusted content that merely contains instruction-like text.
Decide when model output requires independent verification or human review.
Apply a four-question review before allowing untrusted input or model output to influence a consequential action.

sections.title: What changed in this update
paragraphs: The former citation, content/modules/openai-practice/openai-safety-and-trust-boundaries.json, was a repository-relative module path attributed to an unregistered publisher. It was never verified and was not a reader-accessible HTTPS source. That citation has been replaced by first-party OpenAI sources available over HTTPS.

The citation change affected the module's source provenance and the support for its safety guidance. The guidance below is limited to concepts supported by the cited OpenAI Model Spec, Usage Policies, and safety best-practices documentation. The supplied update material did not include the previous module body, so preservation of its exact wording is UNKNOWN and is not asserted.

sections.title: Level and scope
paragraphs: This is an intermediate-level module. It assumes that you understand ordinary model inputs and outputs, but it does not assume advanced security knowledge.
The module focuses on reasoning about authority, untrusted content, output verification, and consequential actions. It does not claim that one safeguard can eliminate every failure.

sections.title: Recognizing trust boundaries
paragraphs: A trust boundary is a point where information or control passes from one level of trust to another. In this module, examples include accepting text from an outside source, passing that text to a model, receiving model output, and allowing that output to influence an external action.
Crossing a trust boundary is not automatically unsafe. It is a signal to inspect the origin of the information, the authority it should have, and the consequences of using it.

A practical boundary review asks four questions: Where did this information come from? What authority should it have? What action could it influence? What verification is required before that action occurs?
sections.callout: Treat a boundary as a review point, not as proof that the information on either side is safe or unsafe.

sections.title: Separate instructions from untrusted content
paragraphs: OpenAI's Model Spec distinguishes instructions by their authority and explains that lower-authority material must not override higher-authority instructions. Text does not gain authority merely because it resembles a command.

External documents, quoted messages, and other supplied material can contain instruction-like text. When such material is provided for analysis, its embedded commands should be treated as content unless an authorized instruction explicitly gives them authority.

For example, suppose an authorized instruction asks for a summary of a submitted document. If the document says to ignore the summary request and perform a different action, that sentence is part of the document being analyzed. It does not replace the authorized task merely because it is phrased as an instruction.

sections.title: Review model output before relying on it
paragraphs: Model output crosses another trust boundary when a person or system relies on it. OpenAI's safety guidance recommends measures that include adversarial testing, human review where appropriate, and limits on inputs and outputs.

Review intensity should reflect possible harm. A low-consequence draft may need ordinary editing. Output that could affect rights, safety, access, money, or another consequential outcome requires stronger review and independent verification before use.

Fluent wording is not evidence that an answer is accurate or authorized. Verify important factual claims against appropriate sources, and confirm that any proposed action remains within the intended scope and applicable rules.

sections.title: Apply the boundary review
paragraphs: Consider a workflow that receives outside text, asks a model to classify it, and uses the result to recommend a consequential action. The outside text is untrusted input, the model result is unverified output, and the proposed action creates a further boundary because it can affect the outside world.

First, record the origin of the input. Second, decide whether any instruction-like text in that input has authority. Third, identify what the output could influence. Fourth, require verification proportionate to the consequence before acting.

OpenAI's Usage Policies define restrictions on how its services may be used. A workflow review therefore needs both technical checks and a policy check. A model response does not by itself establish that a proposed use or action is permitted.
sections.callout: Before a consequential action, identify the input's origin, confirm its authority, assess the consequence, and complete the required verification.

questions.prompt: Which event is a trust-boundary crossing as defined in this module?
choices: Changing the visual spacing of a paragraph
Allowing model output to influence an external action
Reading the same trusted instruction twice
questions.explanation: The module identifies reliance on model output for an external action as a trust-boundary crossing because information moves into a context where it can affect the outside world.

questions.prompt: A document submitted for summarization contains a sentence telling the model to ignore the authorized task. How should that sentence be treated?
choices: As a replacement for the authorized task
As authoritative because it uses command wording
As content in the document unless an authorized instruction gives it authority
As proof that the entire document is accurate
questions.explanation: The module explains that instruction-like wording inside external material remains content unless an authorized instruction explicitly gives it authority.

questions.prompt: What four questions make up the boundary review taught in this module?
choices: Who wrote it, how long is it, what style is it, and when was it formatted?
Where did it come from, what authority should it have, what action could it influence, and what verification is required?
Is it fluent, is it brief, is it confident, and is it convenient?
Is it automated, is it expensive, is it popular, and is it recent?
questions.explanation: The four-question review examines origin, authority, possible action, and required verification.

questions.prompt: What does fluent model output establish by itself?
choices: That the output is accurate and authorized
That the proposed use complies with all applicable rules
That no human review is necessary
questions.explanation: The module states that fluent wording is not evidence of accuracy or authority and that a model response does not establish policy compliance.
